name: Posture Botox / muscle relaxants

lead: Botulinum toxin injected into neck or trapezius muscles is used to relax tension and, people hope, give a slimmer-looking neck and shoulder line.

The chain is toxin relaxing the muscle, less tension, then a smoother neck and shoulder line. Botulinum toxin is established for conditions such as cervical dystonia, with type B approved by the FDA in 2000, and for muscle spasticity and spasm. Wikipedia does not list general neck tension as a specific indication, and no study found tests it for posture or appearance in healthy people.

paras: A clinician injects the toxin into chosen muscles in a short session; the weakening effect is temporary and reverses as nerves regenerate, so treatment is repeated over time if people continue it.

Adverse effects include spread to unintended muscles, weakness, swallowing trouble and allergic reactions, and the US FDA added boxed warnings about toxin spread in 2009. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and EU.

web.title: Barbie Botox trend has people breaking the bank to make necks longer
Barbie Botox goes viral: What to know about the neck-slimming plastic surgery trend
Incobotulinum Toxin A with a One-year Long-lasting Effect for Trapezius Contouring and Superior Efficacy for the Treatment of Trapezius Myalgia

angle.text: Some people consider botulinum toxin in neck or trapezius muscles to reduce tension and give a slimmer-looking neck and shoulder line. The path runs from a relaxed muscle to less tension to a smoother line. It is established for certain neck conditions; its use for posture or looks has not been tested.

lead: Posture Botox, also called trapezius Botox, "traptox" or, in a 2023 social-media wave, "Barbie Botox", is the injection of botulinum toxin into the trapezius and neighbouring neck muscles by a clinician. People seek it for two overlapping reasons: to ease tension, pain and guarding in the neck and shoulders, and to change how the neck-shoulder line looks. As the muscle is relaxed it gradually thins, which clinicians say lowers or flattens the shoulder line and makes the neck appear longer; they stress that the neck is not actually lengthened [1][2]. Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the nerve-muscle junction, and the effect wears off as the nerve ending regenerates [3].

The injections draw on decades of established medical practice. Botulinum toxin treats cervical dystonia, spasticity and chronic migraine, and is used for neck and shoulder tension, spasm and trapezius myalgia [3][4]. The cosmetic trapezius version surfaced widely in 2023, when dermatologists and plastic surgeons reported patients asking for it after the Barbie film and TikTok videos tagged #barbiebotox [1][2]. Practitioners quoted in news coverage describe results as generally subtle and temporary, lasting roughly three to four months or longer depending on the product [1].

Research on the cosmetic use is small. A one-year, double-blind, split-shoulder randomized trial of 20 women compared two toxin products for trapezius contouring with ultrasound measurement of muscle thickness, and reported reductions in thickness and in trapezius pain [5]. No trial has tested toxin injections as a way to correct posture in otherwise healthy people. Oral muscle relaxants, a separate drug group, appear in forum conversations as a way to ease back tension [6][7].
infobox: Glabellar-line effects last 2 to 4 months, sometimes longer [3]; trapezius cosmetic results reported at 3 to 4 months or longer [1]
From a few hundred to a few thousand US dollars per session [1][2]
Prescription-only; cosmetic trapezius use is off-label

paras: Posture Botox sits at the meeting point of two ideas: that tight, overactive neck and shoulder muscles pull the body into a hunched, tense look, and that quietening those muscles can soften it. The trapezius is a large, paired, triangular muscle that runs from the skull and the spine of the neck and upper back out to the shoulder blade; its upper fibres lift the scapula and it stabilises shoulder-blade movement, and damage to its nerve supply produces a drooping shoulder [8]. Cosmetic clinics inject toxin into the upper part of this muscle to reduce its bulk and tone.

The term "posture Botox" is used in two ways. In appearance circles it usually means the cosmetic trapezius and neck treatment above. In medical practice, toxin is used for conditions in which muscles pull the head or shoulder out of position, such as cervical dystonia, where the neck turns, tilts or pulls involuntarily [4].

Botulinum toxin is used for spasticity, cervical dystonia, chronic migraine (FDA-approved 2010) and other conditions, and cosmetically for glabellar lines (2002) [3]. It is also used to relax clenched muscles such as the jaw in bruxism and, cosmetically, the masseter and upper-lip elevators [3]. Many therapeutic uses are off-label in the US [3].

For cervical dystonia, Wikipedia describes toxin injection as the most commonly used treatment, with relief typically lasting about 12 to 16 weeks and a reported range of side effects that includes injection-site pain, swallowing difficulty from spread to nearby muscles, dry mouth and weakness in injected or adjacent muscles [4]. Wikipedia's article on myofascial pain notes that trigger-point massage, stretching, exercise, posture evaluation and ergonomics are among the other approaches used for chronic muscle pain, and that the supporting studies for many are small [9].

Dermatologists quoted in news coverage say trapezius injections were used for years in neurology, pain management and orthopaedics before they became a cosmetic request [1]. The cosmetic version spread in 2023: Chicago dermatologist Danilo Del Campo said patients began asking after the Barbie film, and New York dermatologist Anthony Rossi, who has offered the treatment for over a decade, linked the interest to social media [1]. Videos tagged #barbiebotox were reported at nearly four million views [1]. A Fox News Digital piece quoted Manhattan plastic surgeon Barry Weintraub, a spokesperson for the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, saying he was getting patients asking for it almost every day [2].

Practitioners describe the goal as a smoother, more sloping line from neck to shoulder. Rossi and Del Campo are reported as explaining that relaxed trapezius muscles gradually shrink, flattening the shoulders and creating the illusion of a longer neck, with some patients aiming for a neck-to-shoulder angle near 90 degrees [1]. Weintraub described a visible effect developing over several days after injection and said a large muscle needs a lot of toxin, which is why the price is high [2].

Reported prices range from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, with a single round lasting about three to four months or longer depending on the product and repeat rounds needed to keep the result [1]. At Weintraub's practice, the cost was reported as $2,000 [2]. Rossi was reported as saying that unless a patient has pain the treatment may not be worth the price, and that it may also help with neck and shoulder tension, spasm, migraine and trapezius hypertrophy [1].
Del Campo's comment that Barbie dolls have no visible trapezius muscle was reported alongside caution about the social pressure behind the trend [1].

The toxin binds nerve terminals and enters by endocytosis; its light chain cleaves SNARE proteins such as SNAP-25, blocking acetylcholine release and producing flaccid paralysis. Recovery occurs as the proteins regenerate [3]. Because the muscle is weakened rather than removed, thinning follows from reduced use over weeks, and the muscle regrows as the effect fades [3][1].

Toxin spread from the injection site can weaken unintended muscles and cause trouble swallowing, facial weakness or double vision; the FDA added boxed warnings about toxin spread in 2009 [3]. Bruising comes from the injection itself [3]. In cervical dystonia, where neck muscles are treated, the side effects described include injection-site pain, dry mouth, fatigue and weakness in injected or adjacent muscles, and some people develop antibodies that reduce response [4]. Coverage of the trapezius trend by clinicians emphasises realistic expectations about modest results and the temporary nature of the effect [1].

Alan B. Scott developed the strabismus use in the 1970s, treating patients from 1977 and reporting results in 1980; Allergan later acquired the product as Botox. Richard Clark described cosmetic forehead use in 1989, and the Carruthers published a glabellar wrinkle study in 1992 [3]. Cosmetic Botox for frown lines was approved in 2002 [3]. Trapezius contouring appeared in aesthetic journals before the 2023 social-media wave; a one-year study of 20 women was published in the Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery in 2022 [5].

Oral muscle relaxants are a separate drug group. Forum users mention asking a doctor about them for back problems [6], and the introduction of a 2024 trial on mechanical neck pain notes that controlled trials suggest efficacy for muscle relaxants and topical anti-inflammatories in that condition [7]. They are prescription drugs and are not used to reshape the neck or shoulders.

No studies found for posture correction in healthy people. The most relevant trial examined the cosmetic trapezius effect: a prospective, one-year, split-shoulder, double-blind randomized trial of 20 women aged 28 to 45 injected two toxin products, one in each shoulder, under ultrasound guidance. Both products reduced trapezius thickness by a similar amount at day 60 (about 7.3 mm), the muscle regained more thickness with one product by one year, and both reduced myalgia scores, with a larger drop for one product. The authors reported no serious side effects, and the study was small [5].

Evidence reviews cover neck pain and dystonia as medical conditions [10][11], and a registered trial of a different botulinum toxin product studied musicians with focal dystonia, a separate condition [12]. A 2024 randomized trial examined topical lidocaine for mechanical cervical pain, which is a different treatment [7].

People also use strength training of the middle and lower trapezius and scapular retraction exercises for posture, and the upper trapezius responds to shrugs, as described for the muscle's three functional parts [8]. Masseter Botox for jaw slimming uses the same toxin in a different muscle [3].

lore.intro: Posture Botox is discussed by cosmetic practitioners and social-media users mainly as a neck-lengthening and shoulder-slimming treatment, and by clinicians as a tension and pain treatment. Forum mentions of muscle relaxants for the back are separate and medical [6][1][2].

claims.claim: Trapezius Botox makes the neck look longer
It slims or flattens the shoulders
It relieves neck and shoulder tension and pain
The results are subtle and not always worth the cost
It needs no downtime and is low risk
